prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JERUSALEM (CNN)  -- A rocket fired by Palestinian militants fell on a Gaza home and killed two children, Palestinian sources said Friday, the same day Israel opened three Gaza border crossings for the first time in 10 days. A truck carrying grain enters Gaza from Israel on Friday at the Karni crossing point, one of three Israel reopened. A third child was in critical condition. The children, all girls, were cousins -- the two who died were 7 and 12, and the injured child is 5, Hamas security and Palestinian medical sources said. The rocket struck a house north of Gaza City. In a separate development, the Israeli military said it allowed a Palestinian who was badly wounded by rocket fire Wednesday to enter Israel for treatment. The Palestinian entered Israel through the Erez Crossing between northern Gaza and Israel. Israel closed the crossing for all but humanitarian reasons because of rocket attacks from Gaza into Israel by Palestinian militants. But it opened three other crossings Friday, allowing fuel and commodities into the Palestinian territory for the first time in more than a week. About 80 trucks filled with commodities were expected to cross into Gaza. Among the goods were 400,000 liters of fuel and 120 tons of cooking gas. The decision to open the crossings at Kerem Shalom, Karni and Nahal Oz came after requests from international aid groups and Egypt, said Peter Lerner, a spokesman for the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories. In addition, he said, Israel has no desire to hurt the civilian population in Gaza. Lerner said whether to keep the crossings open would be a daily decision. United Nations assistance programs in Gaza have run out of flour and several essential pharmaceuticals, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said. A tenuous six-month truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired a week ago. Under the Egyptian-brokered deal, Hamas agreed to end militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, and Israel agreed to halt raids inside the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods. In reality, the truce started breaking down two months ago. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza. Since then, dozens of rockets have been fired by Palestinian militants into Israel. Israel Defense Forces said about nine rockets have been launched from Gaza since midnight, pushing the three-day total to more than 110. There are no reports of casualties in Israel. The crossings opened a day after Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met in Cairo and Egypt expressed concern about the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza. Livni criticized Hamas after her meeting with Mubarak. "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population," she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change." Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert has threatened to respond to the escalating violence. He warned Hamas again Thursday in an interview on the Al Arabiya television network and seemed to suggest that time was running out. "We do not want to fight the Palestinian people, but we will not allow Hamas to strike our children," Olmert said. "I did not come here to declare war," he continued. "But Hamas must be stopped -- and so it will be. "I will not hesitate to use Israel's strength to strike at Hamas and Islamic Jihad. How? I do not wish to go into details here."

**JERUSALEM (CNN) —** A rocket fired by Palestinian militants struck a home in Gaza, killing two children, Palestinian sources said Friday—the same day Israel reopened three Gaza border crossings for the first time in 10 days.

At the Karni crossing, one of the three reopened by Israel, a truck carrying grain entered Gaza from Israel on Friday.

A third child was in critical condition. The children, all girls and cousins, were ages 7, 12 and 5, according to Hamas security and Palestinian medical sources. The 7- and 12-year-olds were killed, while the 5-year-old was injured. The rocket struck a house north of Gaza City.

In a separate development, the Israeli military said it had allowed a Palestinian who was seriously wounded by rocket fire Wednesday to enter Israel for treatment. The Palestinian entered through the Erez Crossing between northern Gaza and Israel.

Israel had closed the crossing except for humanitarian purposes because of rocket attacks launched into Israel by Palestinian militants in Gaza. On Friday, however, it reopened three other crossings, allowing fuel and commodities into the Palestinian territory for the first time in more than a week.

About 80 trucks carrying commodities were expected to enter Gaza. The supplies included 400,000 liters of fuel and 120 tons of cooking gas.

The decision to reopen the Kerem Shalom, Karni and Nahal Oz crossings followed requests from international aid organizations and Egypt, said Peter Lerner, a spokesman for the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories. He added that Israel had no desire to harm Gaza’s civilian population.

Lerner said the decision on whether to keep the crossings open would be made daily.

United Nations assistance programs in Gaza have run out of flour and several essential pharmaceuticals, according to the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

A tenuous six-month truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired a week ago. Under the Egyptian-brokered agreement, Hamas pledged to end militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, while Israel agreed to halt raids inside the territory and ease its blockade of humanitarian goods.

In practice, however, the truce began to unravel two months ago. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza.

Since then, Palestinian militants have fired dozens of rockets into Israel. The Israel Defense Forces said about nine rockets had been launched from Gaza since midnight, bringing the three-day total to more than 110. No casualties were reported in Israel.

The crossings reopened one day after Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo, where Egypt expressed concern about the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza.

Following the meeting, Livni criticized Hamas.

“Hamas needs to understand that Israel’s basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn’t mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population,” she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. “Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change.”

Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert has threatened to respond to the escalating violence. In an interview Thursday with the Al Arabiya television network, he again warned Hamas and appeared to suggest that time was running out.

“We do not want to fight the Palestinian people, but we will not allow Hamas to strike our children,” Olmert said.

“I did not come here to declare war,” he continued. “But Hamas must be stopped—and so it will be.

“I will not hesitate to use Israel’s strength to strike at Hamas and Islamic Jihad. How? I do not wish to go into details here.”

**JERUSALEM (CNN) —** Palestinian officials said Friday that a rocket launched by Palestinian militants hit a house north of Gaza City, killing two girls and leaving a third in critical condition. The incident occurred on the same day Israel reopened three Gaza border crossings after keeping them closed for 10 days.

Hamas security officials and Palestinian medical sources identified the children as cousins. The girls who died were 7 and 12 years old, while the critically injured child was 5.

Separately, the Israeli military reported that a Palestinian seriously injured in a rocket attack Wednesday had been permitted to enter Israel for medical care. The patient crossed through Erez, which links northern Gaza with Israel.

Because Palestinian militants had been firing rockets from Gaza into Israel, Israeli authorities had shut the crossings except for humanitarian cases. On Friday, however, Israel reopened Kerem Shalom, Karni and Nahal Oz, allowing fuel and other supplies into Gaza for the first time in over a week. A truck loaded with grain entered the territory through Karni, and approximately 80 trucks carrying goods were expected to pass into Gaza. The deliveries included 400,000 liters of fuel and 120 tons of cooking gas.

Peter Lerner, a spokesman for the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, said the crossings were reopened following appeals from Egypt and international relief organizations. He added that Israel did not want Gaza’s civilian population to suffer. According to Lerner, authorities would decide each day whether the crossings should remain open.

The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said United Nations aid operations in Gaza had exhausted their supplies of flour and several vital medicines.

A fragile, six-month ceasefire between Israel and Gaza’s Hamas government ended a week earlier. The agreement, negotiated by Egypt, required Hamas to stop militant attacks launched from Gaza against Israel. In return, Israel committed to ending incursions into Gaza and loosening restrictions on humanitarian supplies.

In practice, the ceasefire had begun unraveling two months before its formal expiration. Militants increased their rocket attacks, while Israel restarted air raids in Gaza. Palestinian armed groups have since launched dozens of rockets into Israel.

The Israel Defense Forces said roughly nine rockets had been fired from Gaza since midnight, bringing the total over three days to more than 110. No casualties were reported in Israel.

The border crossings reopened one day after Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo, where Egypt voiced alarm over worsening humanitarian conditions in Gaza.

Following the talks, Livni condemned Hamas. According to Israel’s Foreign Ministry, she said Hamas must recognize that Israel’s wish to live peacefully in the region did not mean it would tolerate continued attacks on its citizens. She declared that the situation was unacceptable, that Israel had had enough and that circumstances would change.

Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert had also warned that Israel could respond to the growing violence. Speaking Thursday to the Al Arabiya television network, he again cautioned Hamas and appeared to indicate that its time was running short.

Olmert said Israel did not seek conflict with the Palestinian people but would not permit Hamas to attack Israeli children. He added that he was not announcing a war, yet insisted Hamas would be stopped. He also said he would not hesitate to use Israeli force against Hamas and Islamic Jihad, though he declined to explain how.

counterfactuals.output:
### Two children killed after militant rocket misfires in Gaza as Israel briefly reopens aid crossings

**GAZA —** Two Palestinian children were killed when a rocket launched by militants inside Gaza malfunctioned and struck a home in the enclave, according to local officials and a preliminary Israeli military assessment.

The circumstances could not be independently verified. Palestinian authorities did not immediately identify the armed group believed to have launched the rocket, and no group initially claimed responsibility.

The strike damaged the family’s home and wounded several other people, health officials said. Emergency crews searched the wreckage as relatives and neighbors gathered at the scene.

The incident came as Israel temporarily reopened three border crossings to allow humanitarian supplies into Gaza. Trucks carrying food, fuel, medicine and other essential goods began moving through under security inspections, according to officials overseeing the operation.

Aid agencies have repeatedly warned that Gaza faces severe shortages of basic necessities and have called for crossings to remain open consistently rather than through limited pauses.

Israel said the temporary reopening was intended to increase humanitarian assistance while preventing weapons from entering the territory. Palestinian officials and relief organizations said the volume of aid remained far below civilian needs.

The children’s deaths underscore the risks Gaza’s population faces from both Israeli attacks and rockets fired by Palestinian armed groups from densely populated areas. International humanitarian law requires all parties to distinguish between civilians and combatants and to take precautions to protect civilians.

Calls for an investigation into the blast grew as the victims’ family prepared for burial and aid convoys continued entering Gaza under the temporary arrangement.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed breaking-news article on escalating Israel–Gaza tensions after the expiration of a six-month truce, including rocket attacks, border restrictions, aid shortages, and statements from Israeli leaders.
counterfactuals.output:
# Israel–Gaza tensions surge after six-month truce expires

**GAZA CITY/JERUSALEM, Dec. 24, 2008** — Violence intensified around the Gaza Strip after a six-month ceasefire between Israel and Hamas expired, with Palestinian militants launching rockets toward southern Israel and Israeli forces responding with strikes and tighter border restrictions.

The escalation has increased fears of a broader Israeli military operation in Gaza, where restrictions on crossings have disrupted deliveries of food, fuel, medicine and other essential supplies.

Militant groups fired dozens of rockets and mortar rounds from Gaza in the days following the truce’s expiration on Dec. 19. Israeli authorities reported property damage and injuries in communities near the border, while residents in towns including Sderot were repeatedly ordered into shelters.

Israel carried out airstrikes against what its military described as militant positions, weapons facilities and rocket-launching squads. Palestinian officials reported casualties and said the strikes, combined with border closures, were worsening already severe humanitarian conditions.

## Crossings restricted as supplies dwindle

Israel sharply restricted the movement of goods through Gaza’s border crossings, arguing that normal operations could not continue while rockets were being fired. Crossings were opened intermittently for limited humanitarian shipments, but aid organizations said deliveries remained insufficient for Gaza’s roughly 1.5 million residents.

Shortages of cooking gas, diesel and industrial fuel affected households, transportation and the territory’s main power plant. Hospitals reported concerns about fuel for generators and dwindling stocks of medicine and disposable equipment. Bakeries reduced production as flour supplies fell, while some residents struggled to obtain clean water because electricity cuts disrupted pumps.

Israel maintained that food and medical aid were being admitted when security conditions permitted and blamed Hamas for the deterioration. Hamas and international relief agencies said the broad restrictions were punishing Gaza’s civilian population.

## Both sides blame the other for truce’s collapse

The ceasefire, brokered through Egypt and put into effect in June, had reduced cross-border violence but never eliminated it. Israel said Palestinian factions continued occasional rocket and mortar attacks and accused Hamas of using the lull to rearm and expand its stockpile of longer-range rockets.

Hamas argued that Israel had failed to meet what it considered a central condition of the arrangement: a substantial reopening of Gaza’s crossings. The group also cited Israeli military operations in the territory, including a deadly incursion in early November, as evidence that Israel had broken the truce.

Hamas declined to renew the agreement when its six-month term ended. Israeli officials said the country would not accept continued rocket fire and reserved the right to use substantial force.

## Israeli leaders warn military option is nearing

Prime Minister Ehud Olmert appealed directly to Gaza’s residents, saying Israel did not seek war with Palestinian civilians but would act if attacks continued. He placed responsibility on Hamas and warned that Israel had the military power to change conditions in the territory.

Defense Minister Ehud Barak said Israel preferred calm but was preparing for the possibility of a wider operation. He indicated that military planning was advanced and that the timing of any action would be determined by Israel’s security needs.

Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni likewise argued that no government could tolerate sustained rocket attacks against its population. Israeli officials stressed that warnings to Hamas should not be interpreted as empty threats, although they declined to disclose operational plans.

The increasingly forceful statements came as Israel approached national elections, adding political pressure on leaders to demonstrate a response to attacks on southern communities.

## Civilians brace for further violence

Schools and public facilities in parts of southern Israel adjusted operations as rocket alerts continued. Residents near Gaza were advised to remain close to protected areas, and emergency services increased staffing.

Inside Gaza, families stocked whatever food and fuel they could find, while hospitals reviewed emergency procedures amid expectations of further Israeli strikes. The territory’s health system, already weakened by months of restrictions and intermittent electricity, faced the prospect of mass casualties with limited reserves.

Egypt continued efforts to restore calm and prevent a major confrontation. Cairo also faced calls to open the Rafah crossing between Gaza and Egypt more fully, but Egyptian authorities kept regular passage tightly controlled, citing security and political concerns.

The United Nations and humanitarian organizations urged both sides to stop actions that endangered civilians. They called on Palestinian factions to halt indiscriminate rocket fire and on Israel to ensure sustained access for essential goods.

With no replacement ceasefire in place and neither side showing signs of backing down, the border appeared increasingly close to a large-scale conflict.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a news report explaining why Israel reopened Kerem Shalom, Karni, and Nahal Oz after a 10-day closure despite renewed rocket fire from Gaza, while covering the worsening humanitarian situation and collapse of the Hamas–Israel truce.
counterfactuals.output:
**Israel reopens Gaza crossings as humanitarian crisis deepens and truce unravels**

**GAZA CITY/JERUSALEM —** Israel reopened the Kerem Shalom, Karni and Nahal Oz crossings after a 10-day closure, allowing limited supplies into the Gaza Strip despite renewed Palestinian rocket fire and the near-collapse of an Egyptian-brokered ceasefire with Hamas.

The decision was primarily intended to prevent Gaza’s already severe humanitarian conditions from deteriorating further. The closure had blocked deliveries of food, medicine, fuel and other essentials, forcing United Nations agencies to suspend some aid distributions and leaving Gaza’s power plant short of industrial diesel. Electricity cuts, fuel shortages and restrictions on hospital services intensified across the territory.

Kerem Shalom was opened for humanitarian goods, Karni for bulk commodities such as grain, and Nahal Oz for fuel. Israeli officials described the move as a limited humanitarian measure rather than an end to the blockade or a sign that normal trade would resume. The crossings remained vulnerable to renewed closure if attacks continued.

Israel had sealed the terminals following an escalation that began with an Israeli military operation inside Gaza against what it said was a tunnel intended for cross-border raids. Palestinian militants responded with rockets and mortars, and Israel tightened the blockade. The fighting shattered the relative calm established under the six-month truce that began in June.

The reopening went ahead even as militants launched additional rockets toward southern Israel. Israeli leaders faced competing pressures: to protect border communities and deny Hamas strategic or military supplies, while avoiding a humanitarian breakdown that could draw international condemnation and fuel further instability.

United Nations officials and aid organizations had warned that Gaza’s stocks were running out and argued that its 1.5 million residents should not be punished for militant attacks. Israel maintained that Hamas bore responsibility for the crisis because it controlled Gaza and had failed to stop rocket fire, while Hamas accused Israel of violating the truce through military incursions and by failing to ease the blockade as expected.

The ceasefire had never produced a full opening of Gaza’s borders. Israel said restrictions depended on sustained calm and progress over an Israeli soldier held in Gaza, while Hamas argued that continued closures deprived the agreement of its central benefit.

The limited reopening therefore reflected crisis management rather than reconciliation: enough supplies were admitted to avert immediate shortages, but the underlying blockade, rocket attacks and military confrontation remained unresolved. With both sides accusing the other of breaching the truce, the arrangement was rapidly giving way to renewed conflict.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
